chart.title: Median installed cost
chart.note: Medians from one study; most of their price ranges overlap.

candidates.hook: Heat pump or furnace plus air conditioning? One study's medians were $270 apart.
carries: one study's national medians, not quotes: $6,185 for the heat pump against $6,455 for a gas furnace with central air, and most of the systems' price ranges overlap with the heat pump's
a Canadian model disagrees: it finds heat pumps cost more upfront than gas heating with air conditioning, and come out ahead only over the life of the system
this is the comparison with cooling counted in; against a furnace on its own the heat pump is the bigger number

chart.title: The electrical work

points.label: Field-test sites needing a new panel

chart.note: The field test had 21 sites; the panel figure excludes circuit wiring.

qualifications.text: The sentence names the population: 21 sites, cold-climate prototypes, a field test.

candidates.hook: The quote covers the heat pump. In a 21-site field test, 38 percent needed a new panel.
carries: twenty-one homes in a field test of cold-climate heat pump prototypes, not a national survey, and 38 percent of those sites needed a new electrical panel
the $3,750 to $8,970 is labour and materials for the electrical work only, at the sites that needed it, before the heat pump itself
a typical panel upgrade on its own is put at $1,954 in a larger retrofit database, plus the wiring for each new circuit, so the field test's range is the high end

candidates.hook: A video said the heat pump tax credit runs through 2033. The IRS says it ended in 2025.
carries: the credit was real while it lasted: 30 percent of the cost of a qualifying heat pump, capped at $2,000 a year from 2023
what ended is the federal tax credit, for anything placed in service after December 31, 2025; a heat pump installed before that date is not affected
state and utility rebates are separate programmes and are not what the IRS ended

rejected.reason: two figures from two studies on two baselines ($3,000 against a furnace alone, $6,600 against replacing the same kind of heater); the chart's own note says the tiles are not a range. Alone it reads as a flat heat pump premium, which is the reading the video exists to correct.

repeats the kept s10 finding (about level once cooling is counted) from archetypal model projects that also include hot water, and 'points the same way' depends on s10. Three Shorts on one comparison are one Short.

a single model's conclusion that heat pumps are the lowest-cost option for most households, graded wrong 0.35 against four contradicting studies; a Short cannot carry that disagreement without turning a contested model into a verdict.

the catch is a comparison ('often more expensive than an air conditioner plus gas furnace') that needs the installed medians in s10 and s16 to mean anything, and it carries no figure of its own: a mechanism, not a finding that stands alone.
the $200-$500 gap is wholesale, before installation, and the same study's installed finding (s13) runs the other way; the Short would spend its whole body undoing the figure its eyebrow promises.
the same study and the same table as the kept s10 ($6,185 median), and the parent's own open finding is that 'the study from earlier' is ambiguous, so the sentence does not stand alone as written.
a list of cost drivers (capacity, type, floor area, efficiency, climate zone) with one aside about ground-source, not a finding with a figure.
the question's summary: three comparisons at once, each depending on the sentences before it.

the credit's terms with no end date would tell a 2026 viewer that a credit exists which the IRS has ended; carried inside the kept s25 Short instead, which says both what it was worth and when it stopped.

two things in one scene (whom the federal rebates were for, and three alphabetically-first states with no launch date); the state trio is a cherry-pick, and the programme's rules have since changed (s30), so the scene misleads on its own.

the strongest of the remaining findings, but 'the rebate' needs s26 and s27 to name which federal programme and whom it serves; without them a viewer hears that every rebate stopped paying to switch from gas. Over the cap of three in any case, behind the kept tax-credit Short on the same question.

Mass Save's $8,500 or $16,000 against a $22,000 install is one state's programme, and its qualification is the median everywhere else ($1,327, about 21 percent, s33); a Short on the generous exception sets an expectation the median contradicts.
the counterweight to s32 and meaningless without it; alone the $1,327 median reads as today's rule when the database predates today's programmes.

a Canadian model's barrier finding, graded partly 0.3 on a passage whose own wording limits it ('in most cases', 'despite rebates'), and the parent flags the assertion as stronger than the evidence; too thin to carry a Short.
the question's three-part answer, each part resting on the sentences before it, and its 'usually' is the median from s33.
